archetype: Student who procrastinates until the night before
summary: procrastinates on everything; underneath is perfectionism and fear of finding out they are average

turns.text: I procrastinate on everything until the last night. I know it's bad but I can't stop. How do I fix this?
Let's understand it before trying to fix it, because the fix depends on what's driving it. Think of the last assignment you delayed. What did you feel when you thought about starting it?
A kind of heaviness. Like if I start, it has to be really good, and I don't know how to make it really good yet.
'It has to be really good.' So starting means facing the gap between how good you want it to be and how good it might actually be. What happens when you do it the last night instead?
It's rushed, but then I can tell myself it's only average because I didn't have time.
That's a really honest insight. The last-minute rush gives you an explanation if the result isn't great. What would it mean if you gave something your full time and it still came out average?
That I'm just average. That's what scares me. In school I was the smart one.
So being 'the smart one' became part of who you are, and procrastination protects that identity. How true is it that one average assignment would make you an average person?
When you say it like that, not very. It would just be one assignment. Everyone has average work sometimes.
What might be different if the goal of starting early was not to be brilliant, but simply to see what your real effort looks like?
It would feel less scary. I think the problem was never time management. It's that I'm protecting an image of myself.

summary: phone scrolling ruins focus; scrolling is a way to escape loneliness and boredom in hostel

turns.text: My phone addiction is ruining my focus. I scroll reels for 5-6 hours a day. How do I break the loop?
Five or six hours is a lot, and it sounds like you've already noticed the cost. Before strategies, I'd like to know: when do you usually reach for the phone? What's happening just before?
When I sit to study, or late at night in my room. Basically whenever I'm alone.
'Whenever I'm alone.' That's interesting. What does being alone in your room feel like these days?
Kind of empty. My roommate is always out with his friends. I don't really have a group here yet.
So the phone might be filling an emptiness, not just stealing your time. When you're scrolling, what does it give you that the empty room doesn't?
Noise. People. It feels like something is happening. When I put it down the silence feels worse.

That makes the loop understandable: the silence feels bad, the phone fills it, and then you feel worse about studying less. If loneliness is part of it, what do you think a phone-blocking app alone would and wouldn't solve?
It would block reels but the loneliness would still be there. I'd probably find another distraction.
So the real need might be connection, not just discipline. What's one place in your college where you've felt even a little connected to people?
The coding club I went to once. I liked it but I didn't go back. Maybe the problem isn't my willpower, it's that I'm lonely here.

archetype: Student who constantly compares with toppers
summary: compares self to toppers despite effort; worth tied to rank since childhood

turns.text: Why do I compare myself to toppers even when I try my best? It makes me feel like nothing I do is enough.
That 'never enough' feeling is exhausting. When you compare, what exactly are you comparing: marks, how easily it comes to them, how others see them?
Marks mostly. And how teachers treat them. They get called on, praised, asked to help others.
So it's not only the number, it's the recognition that comes with it. When did recognition and marks first become linked for you?
Since school. My parents would ask 'what did the first rank get?' whenever I showed my report card. Even if I got 90.
So for a long time, your result only meant something in relation to someone else's. How do you feel when you think about that question your parents used to ask?
Small. Like my effort was invisible unless I was first.
That sounds like it really hurt, and it makes sense that the habit followed you to college. If your effort didn't need to be compared to be visible, how would you judge your own semester?
I'd say I improved a lot in programming and I understand circuits much better than last year. I actually did well.
Notice how different that sounds from 'nothing I do is enough'. What do you want to do with that voice that keeps asking about the first rank?
Recognise that it's an old voice from school, not the truth about me now. I can measure myself against who I was last year.

archetype: Student with multiple backlogs feeling ashamed
summary: has backlogs and hides them from family; shame blocks them from asking for help

turns.text: I have three backlogs and I haven't told my parents. I feel like a failure and I can't even open the books.
Thank you for saying this out loud; carrying a secret like that is heavy. When you try to open the books, what goes through your mind?
That I'm stupid. That everyone else passed and I'm the only one. And that if my parents find out they'll be so disappointed.
Three heavy thoughts at once: stupid, alone, and disappointing. Which of them hits hardest?
Disappointing my parents. They took a loan for my fees.
That adds real weight. It sounds like every time you look at the books, you also see the loan and their faces. How did the backlogs happen, from your side?
First semester I didn't understand maths at all. I was too embarrassed to ask in class. Then it kept piling up.
So it began with not understanding, and embarrassment stopped you from asking. Is that pattern, not asking because of embarrassment, still happening now?
Yes. I'm hiding from my parents and I'm also hiding from teachers and friends. I handle everything alone.
That's an important link you just made. If hiding is what keeps the problem growing, what would it look like to stop hiding in one small place first?
Maybe asking my friend who cleared maths to study with me. The backlogs aren't the main problem. Hiding is.

archetype: Student who blanks out in exams
summary: knows material but blanks in exams; pressure of a scholarship makes every exam feel life-defining

turns.text: I study well but I blank out in exams. My mind just goes empty when I see the paper.
That must be frustrating, to know the material and not be able to reach it. What do you notice in your body in the first minute of an exam?
My heart races, hands get cold. I keep thinking, if I fail this, I lose the scholarship.
So each exam isn't just an exam; it carries the scholarship. Tell me what the scholarship means to you.
Without it I can't afford college. My family can't pay the fees. It's everything.
That's a lot of weight to bring into one exam hall. It makes sense that your mind protects itself by freezing. Is it actually true that a single exam decides the scholarship?
Actually no. It's based on overall CGPA above 7.5. I'm at 8.4. One bad exam wouldn't drop me below.
So the rule in your head is stricter than the real rule. How does it feel to hear yourself say 8.4 and above 7.5?
Like I've been treating every exam as a cliff when it's more like a slope.
A slope instead of a cliff. If you walked into the next exam holding that picture, what do you imagine would be different?
Less panic. I'd still care, but the stakes in my head would match reality.

archetype: Student who has lost all motivation for their course
summary: lost motivation for studies; the goal was never theirs, it belonged to a parent

turns.text: I have zero motivation for my course. I used to be a good student. Now I just don't care.
That shift from caring to not caring usually has a story. When do you remember last feeling motivated about studies?
In 12th, preparing for entrance exams. I was working toward getting into a good college.
So there was a clear target then. Whose target was it, mostly?
My mother's dream was that I'd become an engineer. I wanted to make her happy. And I did, I got in.
You reached the goal you were working for. What happened to your motivation right after you achieved it?
It just ended. Like the race was over. Now there's no finish line, just more semesters.
That's a clear picture: the goal was getting in, and getting in has happened. Have you ever had a goal in studies that was fully your own?
Not really. I don't think I ever asked what I wanted to learn. I just did what was expected.
So maybe this isn't laziness. Maybe you're running without a reason that belongs to you. If you were allowed to choose one thing in your field to learn just for yourself, what comes to mind?
Maybe robotics. I never asked myself. I think I need to find my own reason, not more discipline.

archetype: Student at a top internship who feels like a fraud
summary: got a good internship and feels like a fraud; believes success was luck

turns.text: I got an internship at a big company and I feel like a fraud. Everyone is smarter than me and soon they'll find out I don't belong.
That feeling is more common than people admit, especially in a new place. What happened that makes you feel they'll 'find out'?
In meetings people use terms I don't know. I stay quiet so nobody notices.
So staying quiet is how you protect yourself. What do you imagine would happen if you asked what a term meant?
They'd realise I'm not as good as my interview made me look. That I got lucky.
You're saying your selection was luck. What actually happened in your interview?
I solved two coding problems and explained my project well. They said my explanation was clear.
So people who interview candidates for a living saw your actual work and chose you. What makes their judgement less trustworthy than your fear?
Nothing really. I just trust the fear more because it's louder.
Louder isn't the same as truer. If you're an intern, what do you think your team actually expects you to know on day ten?
Not everything. They expect me to learn. Asking questions is probably part of the job, not proof that I'm a fraud.

archetype: Student who never shares projects because they're not perfect
summary: never finishes or shares projects; fear of criticism linked to a harsh school teacher

turns.text: I've started like ten projects and never finished or shared any of them. They're never good enough.
Ten starts shows real energy and curiosity. What happens at the point where you usually stop?
When it's working but looks ugly, or the code is messy. I think, people will see this and laugh.
'People will laugh.' Has that ever actually happened when you showed your work?
In school. A teacher held up my drawing and told the class this is what not to do. Everyone laughed.
That sounds genuinely humiliating, especially as a child. How old were you?
Maybe eleven. I didn't think it still mattered until I said it just now.
Sometimes an old moment keeps making decisions for us quietly. When you imagine sharing a messy project today, whose reaction are you really bracing for?
That teacher's, I think. Not my friends. My friends share half-broken stuff all the time and nobody laughs.
So the audience you fear isn't the audience you have now. What would sharing look like if you were showing it to the people actually around you?
Normal. Just 'here's what I built, it's rough'. I've been protecting an eleven-year-old me from a room that doesn't exist anymore.

archetype: Hinglish-speaking student who games all night
summary: games all night and misses classes; gaming is the only place they feel competent

turns.text: Main raat bhar game khelta hoon aur subah classes miss ho jaati hain. Pata hai galat hai par ruk nahi pata.
Achha hai ki tum khud notice kar rahe ho. Rokne ki baat se pehle samajhte hain: game khelte waqt tum kaisa feel karte ho?
Accha. Main ranked mein top 5% mein hoon. Team mujhe leader banati hai.
Toh game mein tum skilled ho, aur log tumhe lead karne dete hain. College mein kaisa feel hota hai?
Wahan main average hoon. Koi notice nahi karta. Lectures mein kuch samajh nahi aata.
Ek jagah tum leader ho, doosri jagah invisible. Kya ho sakta hai ki game sirf entertainment nahi, balki wo jagah hai jahan tum capable feel karte ho?
Haan yaar. Shayad isliye band nahi kar pata. Game band kiya toh bas ek average student bachta hai.
Ye bahut gehri baat tumne khud kahi. Game mein jo skills use karte ho, strategy, team lead karna, pressure mein decision, kya ye kahin aur bhi kaam aa sakti hain?
Kabhi socha nahi. Shayad college fest ki team ya koi hackathon mein? Strategy toh wahan bhi lagti hai.
Interesting. Toh sawaal shayad sirf 'game kaise chhodu' nahi hai. Tumhe ab asli sawaal kya lagta hai?
Asli sawaal ye hai ki main real life mein bhi capable kaise feel karu. Game chhodna baad ki baat hai.

archetype: Student afraid to try competitive programming
summary: wants to try competitive programming but avoids contests; fear of a low rating defining them

turns.text: I want to get into competitive programming but I keep avoiding contests. What if I get a terrible rating?
So there's something you want, and a fear standing in front of it. What would a terrible rating mean to you?
That I'm not cut out for programming. That I chose the wrong field.
That's a lot to hang on one number. How did the people you admire in CP start out, do you know?
My senior who is a Candidate Master said he was grey for almost a year. I forgot about that.
So someone you admire spent a year at the bottom and it didn't define him. Why do you think a low rating would mean something different for you?
I guess I assume everyone else is naturally talented and I'm not.
That's a belief worth noticing: others are talented, you aren't. What evidence do you actually have for it?
None really. I haven't even tried. I'm judging myself on a contest I never took.
You're right. The rating you're afraid of doesn't exist yet. What would be the purpose of your first contest, if not to prove anything?
Just to get a starting point. A first rating is information, not a verdict.

archetype: Student doing too many things and exhausted
summary: overloaded with clubs, courses and internships; saying yes comes from fear of missing out

turns.text: I'm in four clubs, doing two online courses and an internship. I'm exhausted all the time but I can't drop anything.
That sounds like a lot, and the exhaustion is telling you something. What makes dropping something feel impossible?
Each thing feels important for my resume. If I drop something I might miss an opportunity.
Fear of missing an opportunity. When you look at the seven commitments, which ones would you keep even if they never appeared on your resume?
The internship and the robotics club. The rest I mostly joined because friends were joining or it looked good.
So two things carry real meaning for you, and five are there for how they look. How much of your energy do those five take?
Most of it, honestly. And I'm doing them badly because I'm so tired.
So trying not to miss out is making you miss out on doing the important things well. What do you think a recruiter would value more: seven lines, or two things done deeply?
Two things done deeply. I could actually talk about them in interviews.
What feels true for you now about what you've been chasing?
I've been collecting things to feel safe, not to grow. I need fewer things, done properly.

archetype: First-generation college student who feels behind
summary: first-generation student from a small town; feels behind peers from big cities in English and exposure

turns.text: I'm from a small town and the first in my family in college. Everyone here speaks fluent English and knows so much. I feel so behind.
Being the first in your family to walk this path takes real courage, even if it doesn't feel like that right now. Where do you feel the gap most strongly?
In group discussions. I know the answer but by the time I form the English sentence, someone else has said it.
So you have the ideas; it's the speed of expressing them in English that holds you back. How does that change how you see yourself?
I start thinking maybe I'm not as smart as them. Maybe I don't deserve to be here.
That's a painful leap: from 'my English is slower' to 'I don't deserve to be here'. Are those really the same thing?
No. In maths and coding I'm actually better than many of them. Language is just one skill.
You just separated a skill from your worth. What have you already done, to get here, that most people around you never had to do?
I studied without coaching, figured out the admission process alone, came to a new city alone. My parents can't even read the forms.
Listen to that list. How does it sit next to 'I'm behind'?
I'm behind in one area, but ahead in a lot of others that nobody sees. English is something I can work on, not a judgement on me.
